title: Compliance — SOC 2, HIPAA, GDPR, PCI-DSS, EU AI Act, ISO 42001

questions.question: An enterprise customer asks for proof covering security, privacy, and AI-specific obligations. Your team holds one certificate from last year. What is the gap?
options: One certificate covers every framework forever
Customers never actually verify the documents
A longer certificate title would satisfy procurement
Each framework needs current evidence, reused across frameworks through mapped shared controls
questions.explanation: Procurement wants a living matrix, not a single old PDF. This lesson builds the cross-framework control mapping that produces it.

questions.question: What framework list does PROFILE_MAP return for an EU B2B SaaS customer?
options: HIPAA, PCI-DSS, and Colorado AI Act only
SOC 2 Type I and FERPA only
GDPR + SOC2 + ISO27001 + EU AI Act
questions.explanation: The key (EU, B2B SaaS) maps to exactly those four entries in the local profile table.

questions.question: When does the lesson place EU AI Act Annex III high-risk enforcement?
questions.explanation: The docs distinguish the Act's in-force date from Annex III enforcement on 2 December 2027; Annex I follows on 2 August 2028.

questions.question: Which fine ceilings does the lesson assign to high-risk obligations versus prohibited practices?
questions.explanation: The docs give up to €15M or 3% for high-risk obligations and up to €35M or 7% for prohibited practices.

questions.question: Where should PII redaction occur to prevent an external model from seeing raw data?
options: After the provider has stored the prompt
Only in a report after the response is returned
At the inference layer before the LLM call
questions.explanation: The lesson calls entity recognition and consistent tokenization before the LLM call the defensible standard; post-processing cannot undo exposure.

questions.question: What operational window does the lesson associate with a SOC 2 Type II audit?
questions.explanation: The reference notes describe a SOC 2 Type II window of about 6–12 months, unlike a point-in-time Type I report.
